query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: An active-learning framework that fuses high-throughput DSC/dilatometry measurements with reduced-order machine-learning models informed by DFT and CALPHAD can accurately and efficiently predict melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across multi-principal-element high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys (4–8 principal components) with varied composition and nominally equimolar or near-equimolar ratios in the solid solution state.
generation.intervention: Iterative refinement of a data-driven model using integrated finite-temperature DFT/CALPHAD predictions and high-throughput experimental inputs (DSC and dilatometry) to guide additional targeted measurements and reduce predictive uncertainty across the composition space.
generation.conditions: Samples are heated under controlled inert or vacuum conditions from room temperature to above the predicted melting interval; real-time DSC monitors heat flow, and dilatometry tracks volume changes. Appropriately validated computational thermodynamics (CALPHAD, DFT) seed the model, with each new measurement feeding back into adaptive learning algorithms to improve the prediction performance for both known and unexplored alloy compositions.
generation.structural_mediator: Phase stability and liquid-phase structural configurations influenced by the high configurational entropy in multi-component systems, which in turn govern thermodynamic melting and fusion behavior.
generation.mechanism: By coupling physically-informed input from first-principles and CALPHAD with an active-learning, uncertainty-driven sampling strategy, the model converges on underlying structure–property correlations, refining its predictions of melting behavior and thermodynamic parameters as new data are iteratively obtained.
generation.predicted_outcome: Across newly sampled high-entropy alloy compositions, the approach will predict melting temperature within ±10 K, enthalpy and entropy of fusion within ±5%, volume change on melting within ±5%, and key liquid-phase properties within about 10% of measured values, outperforming standalone high-throughput experiments or conventional computation–experiment pipelines.
generation.baseline: Independent computational (DFT or CALPHAD) predictions or one-shot DSC/dilatometry approaches without iterative data/model feedback loops, whose uncertainty may become large for compositionally complex alloys.
generation.boundary: Relies on sufficiently representative initial datasets and valid thermodynamic databases for each principal element. Complex intermetallics or extreme temperatures outside training ranges may introduce modeling challenges unless additional experiments expand coverage of composition space.
generation.uncertainty: The model’s extrapolation to alloy systems with minimal prior data remains partially unverified; significant deviations might occur if experimental data do not span the relevant chemistry or phase space.

falsification_experiment.design: From the learned model, prospectively design several untested, compositionally diverse HEAs. Synthesize them and measure melting temperature, heat of fusion, entropy of fusion, and volume changes upon melting using DSC, differential dilatometry, and in situ diffraction to compare with predictions.
measurements: Melting temperature and latent heat from DSC
Entropy of fusion from DSC temperature–enthalpy curves
Volume change at melting from dilatometry combined with density measurements
High-temperature phase equilibria via in situ X-ray diffraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured thermodynamic parameters deviate by more than 20% from the predicted values for multiple new compositions, then the adaptive computational–experimental workflow fails to generalize and must be rejected or refined.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe ability to predict and understand phases in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is still being debated, and primarily true predictive capabilities derive from the known thermodynamics of materials. The present work demonstrates that prior work using high-throughput first-principles calculations may be further utilized to provide direct insight into the temperature- and composition-dependent phase evolution in HEAs, particularly Al-containing HEAs with a strengthening multiphase microstructure. Using a simple model with parameters derived from first-principles calculations, we reproduce the major features associated with Al-containing phases, demonstrating a generalizable approach for exploring potential phase evolution where little experimental data exists. Neutron scattering, in situ microscopy, and calorimetry measurements suggest that our high-throughput Monte Carlo technique captures both qualitative and quantitative features for both intermetallic phase formation and microstructure evolution at lower temperatures. This study provides a simple approach to guide HEA development, including ordered multi-phase HEAs, which may prove valuable for structural applications. Explorat

AbstractDeveloping affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system. This study shows that integrating high-throughput screening, multiscale modeling, and experimental validation proves to be efficient and useful in accelerating the discovery of advanced precipitation-strengthened structural materials tune

AbstractThe third-generation thermodynamic descriptions for Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems were performed to construct the reliable thermodynamic database for refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) containing Laves phase. The third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure Cr and V in both solid and liquid phases were established, from which the thermodynamic properties and thermal vacancy can be well described. The thermodynamic descriptions of Ta-Cr and Ta-V over the whole composition and temperature regions were carried out based on the reviewed phase equilibria and thermodynamic data with the CALPHAD (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) approach. Specifically, the thermodynamic parameters of C14 and C15 Laves phases were evaluated by combining the theoretically computed and experimentally measured thermodynamic properties as well as the semiempirical relations. The calculated phase diagrams and thermodynamic properties in Ta-Cr and Ta-V systems according to the present thermodynamic parameters had a nice agreement with the experimental data even down to 0 K, indicating the reliability of the present modeling.Keywords: third-generation thermodynamic description, Ta-Cr system, Ta-V s

decision.trend: Earlier works addressing high-temperature thermodynamics of high-entropy alloys have progressed from high-throughput first-principles and Monte Carlo calculations (PMC6207727) toward more integrated CALPHAD-based screening and design (PMC8282813) for guiding phase stability analyses. Empirical measurements, including calorimetry and in situ techniques, have supported these predictive frameworks by validating melting temperature ranges and phase evolution (PMC6207727, PMC8871103). Recently, third-generation thermodynamic models have been proposed to capture complex intermetallic phases and temperature-dependent behavior across multiple principal elements (PMC8950179). Despite these advances, a comprehensive and scalable approach to simultaneously determine accurate melting temperatures, fusion thermodynamics (enthalpy, entropy), volume changes at melting, and liquid-phase properties over vast multicomponent design spaces remains elusive.
decision.unsolved: There is still no universally adaptable, high-accuracy, high-throughput protocol that can handle the full compositional range of high-entropy alloys for all critical melting-related parameters. Additionally, reconciling predictions from first-principles, CALPHAD, and machine learning models with real-time high-temperature experiments remains a complex challenge. A unifying, systematic methodology that efficiently fuses computation and experiment for broad sets of alloys is lacking, limiting confidence in proposed thermodynamic predictions for new compositions.
decision.lever: An active-learning framework that adaptively fuses high-throughput DSC and dilatometry data with reduced-order ML predictions from combined DFT and CALPHAD inputs, using iterative refinement to optimize models for each new composition. Key parameters include advanced feature engineering of chemical composition and prior high-temperature property data, plus uncertainty quantification to guide further experimental sampling.
decision.why: Building on the success of high-throughput simulations and validation (as demonstrated in PMC6207727 and PMC8282813) and advanced thermodynamic modeling (PMC8950179), an ML-based platform addresses the outstanding need for accurate, scalable, and compositionally inclusive estimation of melting temperature, fusion properties, and liquid-phase behavior across the diverse high-entropy-alloy family. A definitive test would involve prospective prediction of unknown compositions and direct experimental measurement of their melting characteristics. Significant systematic deviations from the predicted melting temperatures, enthalpies, or volume changes would invalidate the approach.
